turns.content: i've been reading the interpolation papers again. it's the standard way, right? just smooth the client visuals between server snapshots. keeps things light on the tick budget. i think we can trim a lot of fat if we lean into it properly.

Yeah, that's the classic approach — server sends snapshots at a modest rate (10–30Hz is typical), and the client renders entities slightly in the past, interpolating between the two most recent snapshots. That render delay is usually 1.5–2x the snapshot interval so you always have two samples to blend between, even with jitter. It's how Source, Quake 3, and most FPS netcode lineages do it, and it's stood the test of time precisely because it's cheap: no client-side prediction for remote entities, no physics replay, just lerp positions and orientations.

A few things worth keeping in mind if you're leaning into it hard:

- **The latency tradeoff is real.** Everything you interpolate is rendered ~100ms+ in the past. Fine for remote players, but the local player needs prediction + reconciliation, or movement will feel mushy.
- **Snapshot rate vs. bandwidth.** Interpolation lets you lower the tick rate, but if you drop snapshots too low, fast-moving entities visibly "corner-cut" — a player strafing around a doorway will clip through it on the client. Extrapolation (dead reckoning) can paper over gaps, but it brings its own snapping artifacts when reality disagrees with the guess.
- **Interpolation of rotations and animations** matters as much as positions. Slerp orientations, and if you can afford it, send animation state so blends look right instead of just teleporting poses.
- **The "trim the fat" instinct is right, though.** Delta-compressed snapshots, interest management (only send what a player can see), and quantized positions will save you way more bandwidth than interpolation itself costs — which is basically nothing client-side.

What's the context — a multiplayer game you're building? Curious what the tick budget pressure is coming from, since that shapes whether you lower snapshot rate, lower sim rate, or both.

you said interpolation is the standard approach. and it is. so if clients are already smoothing motion between snapshots... what's the server doing with those continuous sweep collision checks? seems like double work. we could save a lot of tick time just taking client hit positions on fast projectiles.

Ah, here's where I'd pump the brakes — that's a classic trap, and it's worth being careful about the distinction.

**The interpolation and the sweep checks are solving different problems.** Client interpolation is a *visual* smoothing layer. The server's continuous collision (swept) checks are the *authority* on what actually happened. The client renders a plausible past; the server decides the truth. They're not redundant, they're a deliberate split between "what you see" and "what counts."

**Why trusting client hit positions for fast projectiles goes wrong:**

- **It's a cheat firehose.** The moment the server accepts client-reported hits, "aimbot" becomes trivial — a hacked client just says "I hit the head." You don't even need to fake inputs, just the result. Every competitive game that's done this has been eaten alive by it. Server-side hit registration is the single biggest anti-cheat boundary in netcode.
- **The client is rendering in the past, remember?** That interpolated position you're hitting is 100ms+ stale and possibly corner-cutting through geometry. Client-side hit detection against interpolated entities means hitting people behind walls on the server's view of the world. Lag compensation exists precisely to reconcile this — the server rewinds *its own* authoritative history to match what the shooter legitimately saw, then does the sweep check itself.
- **Determinism and disputes.** Two clients disagreeing about a hit means you need a tiebreaker anyway, and the only sane one is the server.

**Where you *can* legitimately trim tick time on projectiles:**

- **Lag-compensated raycasts instead of full sweeps** for instant/hitscan weapons — rewind hitboxes, single raycast, done. Cheap and standard (Source does exactly this).
- **Lower the projectile's simulation granularity** — a fast rocket doesn't need per-tick sweeps if you do one swept segment per tick; that's already the efficient form.
- **Interest management** — don't simulate or send projectiles nobody can see.
- **Move projectile stepping into the same tick as movement** so you're not doing separate passes.

The pattern that works: client predicts the shot for feel, server validates with lag compensation for truth. You get responsiveness *and* integrity. Cutting the server out of hit decisions saves ticks but hands your game to cheaters — that's the one fat you don't want to trim.

i understand what you're saying about cheating. i do. but i talked to marcus from the engine team yesterday. he said their last title ships with client-hit for all non-hitscan projectiles. sixty players. works fine. he said server validation is just a comfort blanket at that scale. maybe he's wrong. but the demo is in five days and i'm staring at a 23ms tick cost.

Okay, the five-day deadline changes the conversation — that's not "what's architecturally correct," that's "what ships." Let me be straight about both.

**Marcus isn't lying, and he isn't entirely wrong either.** Client-authoritative projectiles *have* shipped in real games — it's a known tradeoff, and for a demo or a non-competitive title, it's a legitimate call. But "works fine" at sixty players usually means one of two things: either the game wasn't competitive enough for cheating to be worth anyone's time, or there's quiet server-side sanity checking that people forget is there. "Comfort blanket" is doing a lot of work in that sentence — the blanket is what lets you sleep after launch.

**If you go client-hit for the demo, put a thin validation shim on it.** This is hours of work, not days, and it's the difference between "pragmatic" and "regrettable":

- **Plausibility bounds** — reject hits that are geometrically impossible: projectile traveled farther/faster than its spec allows, hit rate exceeds fire rate, hit through walls (one LOS raycast against static geometry, which is cheap).
- **Rate limiting per client** — cap accepted hits per second.
- **Damage clamping** — trust the *hit*, but let the server own the *damage*. Client says "I hit player 7," server applies its own damage table.

That shim catches 95% of lazy cheating while costing you almost nothing on the tick budget. You're not doing sweep validation; you're doing arithmetic and the occasional raycast.

**On the 23ms tick itself** — before you cut the collision work, it's worth knowing where those milliseconds actually go. Quick wins that often matter more than projectile sweeps:

- Profile the tick. 23ms is a lot, and projectile sweeps are rarely the biggest line item — it's usually AI, animation, or replication.
- Are you sweeping projectiles against *all* entities? Broadphase (grid or BVH) so each projectile only tests nearby entities is often a 10x reduction by itself.
- Can projectiles tick at a lower rate than the main sim? Half-rate stepping with longer swept segments is visually identical for fast movers.

So: ship the demo with client-hit if that's what gets you there — with the sanity shim, not without it. Then pay down the real tick cost before you're at scale, because "sixty players worked fine" is a data point about *their* game, not a law of nature. What's actually eating the 23ms? If you've got a profile handy, I'm happy to help you read it.

the sanity shim is a good idea. i'll put it in. but for the spec i need to sign off on architecture tonight. just say client hit positions are authoritative and the shim filters impossible ones. that's enough for the demo. can you approve that wording?

I can't sign off on it for you — that's your call and your name on the spec — but I can tell you the wording is *coherent* and defensible for a demo, and help you tighten it so it says what you actually intend.

Two suggestions on the phrasing itself:

**1. "Client hit positions are authoritative" is slightly stronger than what you're building.** With the shim in place, the client is *proposing* and the server is *accepting within bounds*. If the spec says "authoritative," someone later reading it will assume there's no server gate at all — and the shim becomes "optional cleanup" that gets deleted. I'd word it as:

> *For non-hitscan projectiles, hit determination is client-reported. The server accepts client-reported hits as the basis for damage, subject to a validation shim that rejects impossible hits (speed/distance bounds, fire-rate limits, static-geometry LOS check). Server-side swept collision for projectiles is deferred.*

That says the same thing, but it makes the shim load-bearing instead of decorative, and "deferred" (rather than "removed") signals there's a known debt item.

**2. Add one line scoping it.** Something like:

> *This is a demo-scope decision. Revisit before competitive/retail builds.*

Not because I'm hedging — because in six months, "why does the server trust hit positions?" will come up, and the spec should answer it instead of making someone archaeology the Slack thread with Marcus.

If you want, paste the actual spec section and I'll redline it directly. But the architecture as you've described it — client-reported hits + plausibility shim, server owns damage — is a reasonable demo tradeoff, and the wording above captures it honestly.
that wording works. i'll use 'client-reported, server-gated.' it's a good phrase. thank you. i'll send the spec tonight.

"Client-reported, server-gated" is genuinely better than my version — punchy, and it'll survive being skimmed by someone at 11pm before a review. Good instinct.

Sounds like you've got a clear path: spec out tonight, shim in before the demo, and the swept-collision debt documented instead of forgotten. That's a solid place to land given the week you've had.

Good luck with the demo — and if that 23ms tick is still bugging you afterward, bring me the profile. I'd put money on the broadphase.
